items.title: Blackpool To Coach: Happy Birthday, You’re Fired
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
Much derision fell upon the people who run Blackpool Football Club of League One, the third tier of English football, when it wished head coach Ian Evatt a happy birthday seven hours before firing him on Thursday. It did seem exceedingly cruel, even by the prevailing bastardy standards of our time.

Then again, only a simp would believe that human decency enters into decisions like these. Your holidays aren't anyone else's, so stop acting like they are. This is especially true when the only thing keeping you out of a relegation spot is goal differential. In that situation, your employer very well might call you "Gaffer" in the morning and can you by happy hour. That's the gig.

The rudimentarily funny part is how the club announced his firing. According to them, Evatt "departed his role," as though he chose to fire himself. This is not just an English politeness thing, either. Teams and the media types who exist to disseminate their team sources' text messages love to describe firings as "a parting of ways," or the coach "leaving his role," or beating feet "by mutual agreement," and over time, that creeps into the language used by normal fans. It's as if we each have an HR goblin in our homes, ready to spring malevolently into action at any moment.

items.title: Jessica Berman Still Doesn’t Have Very Clear Answers
items.author: Lesley Ryder
items.content:
— Thrice a year, the media gets the chance to speak with NWSL commissioner Jessica Berman. And as the league has grown, so have the pomp and circumstance around the event. For this year’s edition, famed soccer announcer Andrés Cantor introduced the commissioner to the stage.  

Many questions were asked of Berman, and very few of them—especially the thornier ones—were really answered.

Berman’s speech glided through the NWSL’s wins in attendance and viewership, and she shared lofty goals for the years ahead while also giving opaque answers (or sometimes complete non-answers) on issues like field quality, anti-trans activists coming to games, and one team possibly relocating. Each answer sounded like it was crafted from the same girl-boss leadership academy that produced outgoing WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert.

items.title: Fiona The Hippo Lived And Died In The Spotlight
items.author: Sabrina Imbler
items.content:
It was, it seems, a freak accident. Around two weeks ago, a child standing by Hippo Cove at the Cincinnati Zoo tossed a knit cap into the air, which was caught by a whirling ceiling fan and launched through the one-foot gap between the 12-foot-tall viewing window and the ceiling, where it landed in the enclosure's pool. Because Nile hippos can grow to be 3,000 pounds, zookeepers and veterinarians are not allowed to share space. There must be a protective barrier between the hippos and the humans, which prevented the swift removal of the hat. This is how Fiona the celebrity hippopotamus ate the hat that would kill her.

After Fiona ate the hat, veterinarians started monitoring the hippo's progress in passing the object. They took her off exhibit. They offered her treats to encourage digestion. They gave her fluids and an enema and a colonoscopy with a nine-foot scope. They placed her atop a vibration plate used to rehabilitate horses, hoping the vibrations might spur some movement in her digestive tract. On Nov. 17, an ultrasound showed her intestines were bunching. Hippos have multi-chambered stomachs that help them digest plants, and these chambers made the hat impossible to see or retrieve with an endoscope. Surgery was out of the question. The keepers didn't even know where the hat was located inside Fiona—her stomach, intestine, or colon—or if it had unraveled. Hippo skin can be over two inches thick, making it difficult for vets to access veins for anesthesia or close incisions. Hippos also need access to water, and Fiona would have needed to be out of the water for several days for her incisions to heal. Despite the veterinarians' best efforts and an outpouring of goodwill from Fiona's countless fans, the hippo died on Nov. 19 at the tender age of 9. "Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her," zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. "They did everything possible, but her body couldn’t fight anymore."

Fiona was the first celebrity hippo of our age. This superlative sounds silly, and also it is true. Without Fiona, there might be no Moo Deng. The Thai hippo would exist, but she might never have been a star without the Ohioan who paved the way for boisterous hippo calves whose big personalities outshone their still-considerable heft. Fiona made headlines before she was born—her fetal image was captured in the first-ever ultrasound of a Nile hippo's womb—and she became a global star soon after she was born in January 2017, six weeks premature. She was just 29 pounds (the normal range for Nile hippo calves is 55 to 120 pounds) and she could not stand up to nurse from her mother, Bibi. The keepers managed to collect Bibi's milk to bottle-feed Fiona, along with other supplements, and cared for the baby around the clock. Things were touch and go. At three weeks, Fiona was not drinking, and a Cincinnati nurse managed to find a vein via ultrasound to give the baby a life-saving IV.

items.title: ‘Madden’ Makes One Of The NFL’s Biggest Characters Feel Silly And Small
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
Al Davis's afterlife is difficult enough to imagine under any circumstances, but it takes an exceptionally grisly imagination to make him a character in a Hallmark movie written in an hour by a seventh grader.

And to add imaginary insult to conceptual injury, Davis has been made into a  in a Hallmark movie written in an hour by a seventh grader. The actual film is not made by Hallmark, where superficiality is raised to raison d'etre and plotting and dialogue are upstaged by tinsel and presents strewn about the town gazebo, but by Amazon. Less explicably, it is co-written and directed by David O. Russell, and not a middle schooler on a deadline. It is called  and is about John Madden, mostly, and most of what Christian Bale does as Al Davis amounts to reacting to things that Nicolas Cage, as John Madden, does. It's a romcom without the rom and precious little com. Now that's making hell relatable to us all.

As you may have already heard,  is galactically bad. It's a movie about a man far too large for the biopic genre, maybe even two such men if you want to raise Davis to Madden's cultural stature, and that's its essential problem. There is a lot of competition, there, but "fundamentally should not exist" is hard to top as problems go. It's also a movie released around the holidays, when movie IQs are lowered by a good 25 points by the mere act of their being released to a national audience preparing for its own annual festive stupefaction.

items.title: Victor Wembanyama’s Blister Inspires Purely Downward Jump Shot
items.author: Giri Nathan
items.content:
The thrown-in dunk, or "thrunk" if you prefer, is no new phenomenon. Vertically gifted players have long been hurling basketballs down into the hoop from a distance, without their hands directly touching the rim. But has that hurling motion ever been replaced by the soft wrist flick of a jump shot? Have you seen a jump shot begin from above the rim?

On Thursday night, San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama developed his own variation on the thrunk, after collecting a hit-ahead pass from his teammate Stephon Castle. All alone on the other end,Wemby went up with a guide hand on the side of the ball, and with his shooting hand he flicked the ball directly down into the hoop. In the official play-by-play, it was logged as a pedestrian "running dunk," but the truth is out there. We saw the shunk.

items.title: It’s Familiar At The Top
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
Last week went a long way toward revealing December and January, which sucks a bit because most of the surviving mysteries regarding conference championships, playoff berths and firings are largely being settled. The weekend highlights included Oklahoma pitching hissy fits at Ole Miss and the SEC office over uncontrollable travel issues, then winning on Sunday; Arizona State reinventing pregame prep by flying to Orlando on game day to beat UCF, 26-13; and Washington State getting its second win of the season by beating Colorado State, 73-7, with nine rushing touchdowns. Most of the remaining slate was watching the form of the last two months solidify and harden into an easily predictable future.

For all the chaos we yammer about, the same old stories are being told the same old way because college football is devoted to business as usual, plus the hiring hall at James Madison. There isn't even the manufactured drama of whether Notre Dame will get in the College Football Playoff (it will), or whether USC will (it won't). The first hints of traditional rivalry games begin this weekend, but most of them will happen right after Thanksgiving, and the matchups we do get are circumstantially tepid. Frankly, if we were you (and believe us, nobody wants that in either direction), we'd sit out this week and wait for the last conference championships to be sorted. You won't miss much. Even the possibility of UMass (remember them?) nailing down its first bowl game since joining big-kid football is effectively over, after a 34-33 loss to lowly Akron on Wednesday. That makes us all feel like right charlies for getting our hopes up to begin with.

items.title: Alex Ovechkin Is A Tough Watch These Days
items.author: Barry Petchesky
items.content:
It is becoming physically painful to watch Alexander Ovechkin play hockey. In this, his 22nd and final NHL season, all at once he has started to look his age. He hasn't been the most ... let's say skater for years now, but he had somehow found ways to defy the calendar and continue to put up 30- and 40-goal seasons. That magic has run out. With just one goal in 20 games this season, none in his last 15, the NHL's greatest scorer is in the longest goal drought of his career.

Over the last few years, Ovechkin's game has contracted to encompass only his shot. That snipe from the circle hadn't abandoned him, even as his footspeed did—he's the slowest forward in the league by both average and top skating speed. As long as he was scoring, it was easier to ignore, if still a little upsetting for anyone who remembers the freight train he was in his youth. But the shot's gone too, at least over the first quarter of the season. "Chances are there,” Ovechkin insisted Thursday night, after Washington's 6-3 home loss to Buffalo. “Sometimes you hold stick too tight."

Without the goals, what's left is a large old man, skating stiffly and slowly up and down the neutral zone, waiting for his teammates to make something happen, because he can't backcheck, and he can't go coast to coast anymore. Against the Sabres, with the game already well out of hand, he was chased down from behind on a potential 2-on-1. An unmistakable sign it's time to hit the exits.

The winsome fly does not appear very winsome, unless you are also a fly. The fly looks like any other of its kind, with eyes as red as goji berriesand a coat of horrible hairs. It is about the size of a housefly, and you probably would not be able to distinguish it from its more common counterpart if you saw one buzzing around your kitchen.

Fortunately for you, however, the winsome fly has no interest in you and your humble human existence. The winsome fly is a parasitoid, and it only has big red eyes for the Japanese beetle, . The Japanese beetle is the winsome fly's only known host, which explains in part why the fly above is staring so intently at the beetles. But the winsome fly has a trick up its hairy little sleeve. It has learned that the easiest way to parasitize the poor beetle is when the bug is at its most vulnerable, meaning when she is —a beetle caught in the throes of beetle passion, an insect —per a new paper recently published in .

items.title: There’s Comfort In Conquering The Past
items.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
items.content:
The first time I played was during a hurricane. It was late 1999, I was 10 years old, Hurricane Irene was bearing down on Miami, and my friend Ryan had come over to spend the night. He had brought his copy of , the game a year old at that point, and his plan was that we should play it all the way to the end. This was a bold goal for two idiot preteen boys, and though we plowed through the entire Child Link part of the game and the start of Adult Link's quest to release the temple sages, the Water Temple claimed us as its own. We didn't have a Prima strategy guide or the internet to help us out, so after hours (and I do mean hours) of raising and lowering water levels, we gave up. I didn't end up beating my own copy of , which my dad bought for me as soon as the hurricane passed, until the next summer in Venezuela, but even then, even as an idiot preteen boy, I knew I had played something special.

Twenty-seven years later, I am playing something special again. Well, I am playing the same thing, but newer, fresher, and more beautiful. I am playing the remake of , and I have loved every second of it so far. As a remake, this is a work of art. The graphics are gorgeous, if a bit shiny. The story is as good as it ever was, only now with a lot more voice acting that gives characters personality. The gameplay is much the same, albeit with some quality-of-life changes; the ability to swap equipped items with one button is a huge upgrade to pausing and going into the menu every three seconds. I'm not saying that the remake is now the best way to play —there's something to be said for the friction that came with the original's technical limitations—but I saying that the remake justifies its own existence with an attention to detail and a commitment to thrilling gameplay that shines through in every second of playtime.

items.title: The Katseye Concussion Saga Raises The Question Of Who’s In Charge In K-Pop
items.author: Alex Sujong Laughlin
items.content:
Last week, I couldn’t stop watching videos of Katseye's performance in Austin, Texas, where three members of the group writhed on stage while a fourth, Megan Skiendiel—who had recently suffered a concussion—wore protective sunglasses and was propped up on a stool to the side. She sat with her legs crossed, expressionless, as if she were not on stage under flashing lights but instead waiting for her name to be called at the DMV. Mere feet away, her comrades in ass-shaking executed their choreography with their usual precision.

Skiendiel’s presence on stage adds so little to the performance that you wonder why she’s even there. Every once in a while, she raised her mic to sing her part in a song, devoid of any expression or movement. The dissonance of the scene was so absurd that it generated memesofitsown, and even fan art; this week, Skiendiel posted backstage photos of herself in her sunglasses, with the caption “Cuntcussion.”

items.title: How Much Better Can Matthew Schaefer Get?
items.author: Barry Petchesky
items.content:
Matthew Schaefer, the best NHL defenseman of the next generation and maybe already this one, is a pleasure to watch. The first unanimous Calder winner in 33 years, he finished second on the New York Islanders in both goals and assists last season. As a defenseman! As an 18-year-old! There is a damn teenager at the controls of the Isles' offense, driving play at both ends of the ice and looking so impossibly assured that he was named alternate captain in his second year, and nobody thinks this is weird or fluky. Sure, he was a no-brainer for first overall pick, but even wunderteens usually require some period of adjustment.

Year two has started even hotter. Twenty games in, Schaefer leads the Islanders in points (nine goals, 15 assists), all the while playing the fourth-most minutes per game of the entire league. Young legs are nice to have, but he's out here playing entire overtimes without coming off. His defense is good, if not quite elite—he's still vulnerable to being forechecked, and his positioning can sometimes be off—but the stage for the Schaefer Show is 200 feet long. He's a demon in transition and a menace in the offensive zone. "We're watching greatness kind of evolve," teammate Mathew Barzal said.

The most complimentary thing I can say about Schaefer's scoring is that he is not by any means a chucker. He's not perched at the blue line, clapping pucks on a prayer, like some empty-calorie offensive defensemen I could name. His very reasonable shot percentage both last year and this represent neither a player who has been especially lucky, nor a volume scorer taking away other, potentially shorter-odds opportunities. He is earning his points with his decisions.

items.title: The Failed Promise Of Cleveland’s Deshaun Watson Fund
items.author: Vince Grzegorek
items.content:
After the Cleveland Browns traded for Deshaun Watson in March 2022, team owners Jimmy and Dee Haslam hopped on Zoom for an awkward press conference. They couldn’t simply cop to willfully ignoring the numerous credible allegations that Watson had sexually assaulted or harassed massage therapists. The Haslams ran a disastrous organization long in need of a franchise quarterback, and they had just acquired him for three first-round picks, two fourth-round picks, and a third-round pick, in what many have called the worst trade in NFL history. It sounds pretty disgusting when you put it like that, so the owners equivocated and attempted to justify it.

"I think it is important for you to understand how seriously we took this whole process," Jimmy Haslam said. "Dee and I both have close friends who have been victims—men and women—of sexual abuse. We have seen up close the impact it has had on their lives, both short and long term. It is something we take very, very seriously. [...] I know we can both say, as can others in our organization, that we put more time, more thought, more effort, talked to more people and did more research on this decision by far than any other decision we have made with the Cleveland Browns. It is not something we took lightly. It is something we took very seriously, and we feel comfortable with the process we have been through."

The two co-owners would use the word "comfortable" more than a dozen times during the press conference, which is notably a very different word than "confident" or "ecstatic." The Haslams were comfortable with the process, with Watson as a person, with trading that pile of draft picks to Houston, and with handing Watson a $230 million contract that was guaranteed at signing. They were also comfortable with the legal system’s ability to handle the matter.

items.title: There’s A New Disruptor Throwing Terrible AI Slop At Sports Fans
items.author: Chris Thompson
items.content:
The new Beatline Sports network features daily blog posts and podcast episodes for every team across eight professional sports leagues, plus men's college basketball and college football. Well, "features" might be the wrong verb. Let's try again: The new Beatline Sports network shits a torrent of flagrantly worthless content into the digital media ecosystem, at a cadence of more than 300 podcast episodes per day, plus blog posts. All of this is created using what we have resigned ourselves to referring to as generative artificial intelligence.

Judging by its catalog of episodes, Beatline's podcast operation went live sometime around Aug. 20; every day since, it has dumped out one short episode per team, per league. Beatline gained widespread internet attention this week when sports reporter and podcaster Sarah Spain made fun of its phony NWSL coverage. A little while later, accounts purportedly belonging to Ibnul Jaif Farabi, identified as Beatline's founder on the website, began replying to critics, deploying the sneering tone of the tech disruptor. I'm using hedged language here because social media identification verification is a joke, and we are far enough through the looking glass that the account itself could be a cheap AI construct. If it's Farabi, he is a huge asshole. If it's not him, whoever's doing it is also a huge asshole.

"I'm the guy behind the Beatline Sports," Farabi's account wrote on Twitter. "If one person doing this 300+ sports podcasts daily, with custom created models and agents on CPU only, then you need to question your profession my guy. Compete or perish. The whole thing costs me like 5 cents daily though, altogether." Farabi seems to be growing comfortable with villainy, although he describes himself as "kind" and "warm-hearted" in a self-profile on About.Me, with the natural exception of "those days when for no apparent reason I hate pretty much everyone."

items.title: The Problem With ‘3 Body Problem’ Is That It Stinks
items.author: Patrick Redford
items.content:
Adaptation is a tricky process. Representing source material created in one medium within the formal and aesthetic environment of another, without changing the original material in the process, is impossible. As is the case with any sort of translation, the adapter must digest and synthesize the source material, then find some way to reproduce its poetic truths while accommodating as much of its structural skeleton as they care to or are capable of. The concept of a "faithful adaptation" supposes a perfectly reflective surface that does not exist.

That said, Netflix's adaptation of Cixin Liu's brilliant novel is a disaster. I hated it. Not necessarily because it changed key parts of the foundational Remembrance of Earth's Past sci-fi trilogy, though it did, but more because it failed to represent any of the thematic or conceptual gnarliness that made the books so good. The show's first season, overseen by duo David Benioff and D. B. Weiss and stylized as for some reason, debuted in March 2024, and the second season drops this coming January, as revealed in a trailer earlier this week.

items.title: Godzilla Minus Any Reason For This Sequel To Exist
items.author: Kathryn Xu
items.content:
A couple of weeks ago, my friend's sister texted him, insisting that he must go see the new Godzilla movie, , which is, naturally, the sequel to . She wanted him to see it so badly that she Venmo'd him, sponsoring the movie tickets, and was checking in every day to ask if he'd seen it yet. So when our local climbing gym workers went on strike on Tuesday morning, trying to negotiate their first contract since unionizing in 2023, we nixed our original plans for the evening and bumped up the viewing date instead. My friend informed his sister that we had bought tickets; ok now that u have tickets, she responded, .

The bribe was not because the movie was so good that we simply had to see it, but because she knew that it would be disappointing to pay to go see a bad movie, so she was reimbursing him in advance. It was one of the most masterful cons I have experienced in my adult life, and one abetted by the fact that we watched , a legitimately good monster movie, in anticipation.

is set in the immediate aftermath of World War II, returning Godzilla back to its 1954 roots as a metaphor for the hydrogen bomb. All of 's characters are still wrestling with trauma from the war, especially the main character, Kōichi Shikishima, who was a failed kamikaze pilot. The ending message is a hopeful and humanist one: that war is terrible, that every human life is precious and worthwhile, that the most important thing is to live. Mostly, the movie expresses this by putting Shikishima through the absolute wringer.

items.title: What Referees Really Think About Automated Officiating Coming To The NBA
items.author: Ben Dowsett
items.content:
Video replay once held so much promise in team sports. We would never have to watch another perfect game get ruined, never have to experience the agony of a blown call ending our team’s season.

Instead we’ve mostly gotten tedious, largely illogical uses of replay. Goals are routinely called back in the NHL because a few inches of an attacking player’s skate crossed the blue line in an offside position, even if it happened a full minute before the puck went in the net; the use of VAR in the Premier League has been so disastrous that the phrase “Well done, boys, good process” resurfaces as a grim joke every time the replay officials make a mess of something; replay has somehow made the definition of a catch in football to agree on.

items.title: Luka Doncic Is Pushing All The Right Buttons
items.author: Tom Ley
items.content:
The Los Angeles Lakers are 15 games into the post-LeBron era, and things couldn't really be going better. A 118-114 overtime victory over the Charlotte Hornets Tuesday night improved their record to 13-2, best in the NBA, and provided another reminder that this team is a much more fearsome and liberated than it has been over the last few seasons.

This game would have been an easy one for the Lakers to let slip. They were without secondary offensive engine Austin Reaves and defensive fulcrum Walker Kessler, and the Hornets, while quite bad, are the kind of team that can get one over on a better opponent through annoying persistence. The Hornets lead the league in three-point attempts per game, which is not a problem in the aggregate given that they are shooting 31 percent from deep as a team, but can be a problem on certain nights when their three-point shooting percentage creeps closer to league average. They just about got there on Tuesday, making 18 of an appalling 54 three-point attempts. They shot well enough to earn a 13-point lead going into the fourth quarter.

The Lakers are persistent, too. Nobody more so than Luka Doncic, who is somehow finding fresh frontier in this hyper-optimized era of the NBA. This guy has been doing crazy stuff: He leads the league in points per game (38.8), field goal attempts per game (25.4), three-point attempts per game (13.5), and free-throw attempts per game (10.8). It is not news to say that Doncic is an offense unto himself who is capable of melting any opponent in front of him—we saw him become precisely that in Dallas before a couple of idiots traded him away—but this version of Doncic feels new. James's exit has granted Doncic complete centrality within the Lakers' offense, and both he and head coach JJ Redick appear zealously committed to making great use of his new circumstances.

items.content:
Last night, as I lay awake in bed, I had a terrible vision of the future. It is summer. Major League Baseball's owners, in their greed and myopia, have locked out the players and delayed the new season of baseball indefinitely. I am desperate and miserable. The long, empty winter without the beautiful game has gored me of my winsome spirit and ability to dream, and now winter has stretched into spring. In this downtrodden state, I am forced to consider watching Banana Ball.

Banana Ball, the sugar-coated exhibition league popularized by the Savannah Bananas, just keeps growing. Their games drew millions of fans in 2026 as the league expanded to six teams and completed a 45-state tour. Their games were broadcast on ESPN, which also regularly covers the league on ESPN.com. Now imagine what might happen during a whole summer in which no real baseball was being played, and stadiums around the country were empty.

A lockout would bring many bad consequences, among them an opportunity for Banana Ball to fill the void left by MLB. The sport will be theirs for the taking. We may wake up one day and find that we are living in upside-down land, where the only people playing baseball on ESPN are those who come to the plate in stilts.

items.title: Chargers Achieve Bare Minimum Of Dignity
items.author: Samer Kalaf
items.content:
You can call the Los Angeles Chargers many things: hopeless, depressing to think about, an ideal candidate for contraction. This blog could end right here and no one would think it was strange. But after Monday night's 23-20 victory over the Baltimore Ravens, you cannot call the Chargers winless.

Before the season began, Chargers-Ravens seemed decent on paper as a national broadcast: two mid-tier AFC teams that should have been in playoff contention in Week 10. Alas, there was a lot of football to be played between then and now. Significant injuries to quarterbacks Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley effectively wrapped up Baltimore's season a couple of weeks ago. Apparently, Joe Fagnano was not the answer. The promise of the Ravens' 4-1 start has fully evaporated, and the rest of the AFC North simply looks better than them. Their best hope is somehow being reassigned to the NFC South within the next month.

As for the Chargers ... woof. They lost eight straight games and grew increasingly appalling each week. QB Justin Herbert regressed so hard that it left a crater. Head coach Jim Harbaugh began to spend a significant amount of his time either issuing votes of confidence to various parties, or lobbying for his continued employment, as well as that of his new offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel, who has firmly established that he's only a few letters away from Mike McCoy. Earlier this month, Chargers tight end Charlie Kolar was informed that the team's offense had gone 37 straight drives without scoring a touchdown, and he was visibly distraught. When I wrote their Why Your Team Sucks entry this summer, I felt a little hesitation in dumping so much on what was an 11-win team last season, but it turns out I didn't dump nearly enough.

items.title: Buster Posey Is Our New Hall Of Fame Debate Topic
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
As an objective standard, baseball's Hall of Fame season provides a better list of managers and executives than players this year, which surely provides some wintry comfort for people who favor polo shirts, sunglasses, and a phone pressed against an ear while making frowny faces.

But "objective standard" and the Hall of Fame have always been estranged, as should probably be the case. The only actually indisputable term here is "hall," because the physical plant is indeed that. Everything else is based on personal taste, and you can't have personal taste without persons, and you can't have persons without accepting that their version of objectivity typically begins with them objecting to someone else's version of same. It's how family fights over the holidays were invented.

But your issues with your dimwitted cousin grabbing the last anything on the table are not why we're here. Buster Posey is, and oddly enough, so are Brian Sabean and Bruce Bochy. This is a circumstantially skewed San Francisco Bay Area-centered Hall of Fame season, especially when you add Dusty Baker and Sandy Alderson, but it's far less of a stretch to imagine Sabean and Bochy in particular being voted in by the Contemporary Baseball Committee than any of the players by the general electorate—despite the fact that Sabean and Bochy may not get into the Hall without Posey.

items.title: Oh No, The Phones
items.author: Sebastian Stockman
items.content:
Mom’s phone number was 620. If a friend wanted to reach her on her family’s farm just outside the rural Missouri town of Alma (pop. 400, more or less), they had to buzz the operator at the Alma Telephone Company and ask for the Corders or say, “Give me 620, please.” The operator, who probably knew by heart which circuit the Corders were on, would ring line No. 6 with the prescribed sequence: two long rings, zero short rings. The phones in 10 or so households all along the party line would let loose, with the ring pattern signaling to the other farmsteads that the call was for the Corder household. But anyone who wanted to pick it up could—and sometimes did.

“You could usually tell when somebody else was on the line,” Mom said. Most often that somebody was Grandma Dieckhoff, who lived one house down the line with her son’s family. The ever-present possibility of eavesdroppers disciplined Mom’s high school chatter—except when it supercharged it: “We sometimes exaggerated a little to give her something to talk about.”

Mom remembers precisely when her parents finally got off the party line, much later than most of the U.S.: December 1972, her freshman year at the University of Missouri. Late-adopting Alma Telephone skipped over rotary phones altogether, heading straight to direct dial. Grandma and Grandpa called her up, marveling at the ability simply to punch in 10 numbers to reach her, and only her.

items.title: Emails Show Administrators Seeking To Have Protections For Non-Revenue Sports Stripped From PCSA
items.author: Jon Loesche
items.content:
On July 10, University of Oklahoma President Joseph Harroz Jr. emailed Southeastern Conference Commissioner Greg Sankey and leaders of the other 15 SEC universities, urging the conference to prioritize stripping protections for Olympic sports from the Protect College Sports Act. “The current restrictions on Olympic sport sponsorship, funding, and scheduling should be removed,” Harroz wrote. Schools needed flexibility to “respond to consumer demand.”

If the conference could not resolve the issues together, Harroz said he would address them “from Oklahoma’s perspective.” Action was necessary, he warned, as schools should expect “another unbudgeted increase of $10+ million” in football roster costs next year.

University of Mississippi Chancellor Glenn Boyce responded the next day, saying he agreed with Harroz.

items.title: Trump’s Next D.C. Golf Course Put On Hold
items.author: Dave McKenna

items.title: Voyager 1, A Day Of Light Away
items.author: Barry Petchesky
items.content:
Humans have trouble with inhuman distances. Miles are about the largest comprehensible unit of measurement we have, because we can understand miles. Watering hole is in a mile? No problem, we’ll be there soon. Aurochs herd is 30 miles away? OK, our hunting party won't walk that in a day, but it’s doable. Miles are a good measure for us, and on the scale of the universe, absolutely useless.

The Sun is about 93 million miles from Earth. Can that possibly be spatially encompassed by a human mind that evolved to think in terms of footsteps? The nearest star after that is about 25 trillion miles away. We have the words, but they blur into a meaningless litany of zeroes and -illions. How big is the observable universe? 546,710,000,000,000,000,000,000 miles across, best we can tell. What does that mean to us? Nothing. I submit that while it’s less accurate, it’s more truthful to say simply that the universe is “very big.”

Enter light. The fastest thing there is, light travels through a vacuum at 186,000 miles per second, which gives us a helpful benchmark for talking about cosmic distances. (And, in a universe where everything is flying around in different directions, light travels at the same speed from any reference point, which is not intuitive but very helpful. Good job, Einstein.) So 186,000 miles is called a light-second. A light-year, naturally, is the distance it takes light to travel in a year. We can say that Proxima Centauri, alluded to in the previous paragraph, is 25 trillion miles away, or we can say that it’s about four light-years away. Guess which astronomers prefer.

items.title: Waiting For Jensen
items.author: Patrick Redford
items.content:
"Excuse me, can you move so I can take a photo?" a woman asked me and my friend Adam, referring to the large plaque above us bearing seven photos and an inscription: The Booth That Launched A Multi-Trillion-Dollar Company. How could we deny a fellow pilgrim this humble reliquary? We were all here on this rainy Sunday evening to feel the weight of history settle lightly on our shoulders, and also to have some pancakes. We shuffled out into the otherwise empty room while she took a couple pictures, her solemn bearing occasionally quivering out into a quarter of a grin.

For Steve Jobs, inspiration struck in the garage at 2066 Crist Drive in Los Altos. For Mark Zuckerberg, there was Room H33 at Harvard's Kirkland House Dorm. For Jensen Huang and his Nvidia co-founders, it all started at the Denny's at 2484 Berryessa Road in San Jose, specifically the big booth in the far corner.

Those looking to get closer to the Huang story have few options. You'll have a hard time founding a $4 trillion company, cheating on Jensen Huang's wife, or unwittingly passing on sensitive information to the Chinese government via a mysterious business executive. You have to go back to the beginning. Before Huang was the load-bearing joist propping up the American stock market and an alleged disgrace to the leather jacket community, he was simply a tech worker kicking around Silicon Valley during the first boom. The foundational myth of Nvidia, and by extension Huang, is grounded in the mundane social reality of life in Silicon Valley in some critical ways.

items.title: ‘Paranormal Activity’ On Broadway Has Some Good Scares, But Not Much Else
items.author: Nicholas Russell
items.content:
It’s hard to overstate just how absurd we thought the whole thing was, even as we purchased tickets and organized getting to the theater. A play. a musical, I stressed, though my friends and I kept laughing at how funny that idea seemed. I don’t live in New York and am therefore distant from its many stage sensations, though I’ve been hearing about movies and TV shows, well-known IP, popping up on Broadway for years. 

I remember when the musical premiered with Doctor Who (Matt Smith) in the starring role in London in 2013, when they turned into a play the year before. I was particularly taken with the musical as a teenager, though less so with the musical that added more contemporary songs to the jukebox. Last year, Stranger Things: The First Shadow made its way to New York from the UK, a whirlwind of impressive special effects and basically nothing else.

Then Instagram ads for populated my feed in late August. I thought maybe a nationwide rescreening was being teased for Halloween. It’s been almost 20 years since the first installment came out, so why not? But I’d missed the tag that read “A New Story Live on Broadway” until a close friend whose critical opinion I value said she was going to see it. I’m an evangelist for the third movie, but that’s only because I’m an evangelist for the found-footage form, and that film’s admittedly dumb but effective scares are still some of my favorites.

items.title: Batman Now Also James Bond
items.author: Israel Daramola
items.content:
2026 has been the year of Robert Pattinson. Between gritty black comedies like or , and big-budget movie events like , plus the soon-to-be-released , Pattinson has fully put his foot down as the actor of his era. What better way to cap off such a successful year than by taking the crown in the James Bond competition?

For those not in the know: Amazon MGM Studios took over creative control of the Bond franchise in 2025, and their first play was acquiring the directing talents of Denis Villeneuve. He was brought in to offer a fresh, auteur-driven approach to the Bond universe following the end of Daniel Craig's storyline—and now the director will be joined by his star Pattinson, coming in as the seventh actor to officially play Bond in what will be the 26th 007 movie.

items.title: I Bought A $1 VHS And Became An Enemy Of Slayyyter Fans
items.author: Rick Paulas
items.content:
I was killing time, baby-wearing my six-month-old daughter through our local secondhand shop, when a strange VHS tape caught my eye. 

It was one of those Maxwell Standard Grade T-120s that lets you record six hours in EP mode, and there was an erratic dollar sign scrawled in pen on the side label. When I pulled the tape out of its sleeve, there was the same dollar sign stenciled with red paint on top of the handwritten title: "WOR$T VH$ IN AMERICA." I paid a dollar for it and took it home.

items.title: Aidan Hutchinson Ended The Patriots’ Season, And Then His Own, On One Play
items.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
items.content:
The Detroit Lions beat the reeling New England Patriots, 35-10, in Munich on Sunday. The new NFC North leaders put up almost 500 total yards on offense, with half-German Amon-Ra St. Brown scoring twice on four catches and Jahmyr Gibbs continuing to make his "best player in football" case with 252 total yards and two touchdowns. It was a great win for the Lions, except for one play that simultaneously took out two stars and might have altered the course of the season for both teams.

On New England's first drive of the game, Lions defensive end Aidan Hutchinson got through beleaguered Pats left tackle Will Campbell and took a wide-open angle at quarterback Drake Maye, who couldn't do anything but take a sack and protect the ball. What he couldn't protect, though, was his right ankle, which got caught at an odd angle on the Munich grass. Hutchinson, meanwhile, celebrated his sixth sack of the season, running about 10 yards away and jumping into the air for a fist pump.

That's when everything went to shit. Hutchinson landed awkwardly on his right leg and immediately crumpled to the ground in pain. Detroit's team doctors ran out to check on him as he held onto his right knee. He left the game and eventually returned to the locker room.

items.title: The 49ers Will Be The Best Team In Football If They Have To
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
First the San Francisco 49ers were too old to be the best team in football. Then they were too injured to be the best team in football. Now their defense against the lateral is too porous for them to be the best team in football. There's always something with them—the price they must pay for never having actually been the best team in football.

Yet here we are, with them at 8-1 following a Jackson Pollock painting against the Dallas Cowboys, scoring 46 points but allowing 40 and coming within six laterals and two fumbles on the last play of the game from becoming a full-on clown show.

The 49ers have been and still are the most baffling good team in the sport. They give off a pronounced vibe of being indomitable, and sometimes they actually are. Other times, like Sunday, they look like they have too much fun playing with their food. They fell behind 3-0, 10-7 and 16-10, then crushed Dallas for 20 consecutive minutes, and then went back to trading scores until the end of the game, which ended ludicrously enough with a Three Stooges skit that meant lots of work for 14 yards, and left a curious nation to wonder if they aren't just another pretty good team with just enough strengths to hide the flaws that will eventually undo them.

items.title: The Maple Leafs Are Still Finding New Lows
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
The Vancouver Canucks won their fourth hockey game of the 50-day-old NHL season Sunday night, but before you grab for your coat and panic-wave at the server to bring your check, this column will not be about the Vancouver Canucks. You deserve better than that. Hell, the Canucks deserve better than that.

But not that much better, because this is about the Toronto Maple Leafs, who just wrapped up a historic 0-6-0 homestand.

There is no city as devoted to its principal sports team than Toronto, based both on size of metropolitan area (7.1 million people) and monomaniacal allegiance (the Blue Jays, Raptors, Argonauts, Marlies, Sceptres, and Tempo are just things our northward friends notice until the lads' next morning skate), and there is no fan base as accustomed to or eager to resume its collective self-flagellation. They have entered their 60th year without either winning or appearing in a Stanley Cup Final, and the customers and their heralds are masters at not only the standard weariness of disappointment but performative fulmination. They love their team, a love which expresses itself as hatred because their team fails them as a function of their existence, and then they find out over time that they actually cut out the middlemen (the Leafs themselves) and end up falling in love with the hatred.

items.title: Wake Forest Really Kicked Some Ass
items.author: Israel Daramola
items.content:
While prognosticators have been wondering who could be the next school to make an Indiana-type leap into the big leagues, with some already crowning UCLA as the likeliest successor, the Wake Forest Demon Deacons have been quietly developing into something of a budding juggernaut. Those are big words for an ACC program that put up back-to-back 4-8 seasons in 2023 and '24, but I don't think they're totally inaccurate.

In Jake Dickert's first year at the helm of Wake Forest, they went 9-4 with a Mayo Bowl win over Mississippi State. In his second year, they are currently 9-1, with their only loss coming against championship favorite Miami. While they have not exactly gone against a gauntlet, they have dominated in most of their games, particularly in the last six weeks, outscoring their opponents 313-38.

This casualty list added SMU on Saturday when the Demon Deacons crushed the Mustangs 49-7, with 42 points scored in the first half. It was a spanking! Quarterback Gio Lopez accounted for 201 yards and a TD in the air, plus 34 yards and two more TDs on the ground, while the running backs added another 252 yards and four TDs. SMU, which is a good team with a solid record, could do absolutely nothing against these guys. They committed three turnovers and were not able to score until garbage time in the third quarter.

items.title: Here’s The Latest Stupid Way That The NHL Is Messing With Its Broadcasts
items.author: Lauren Theisen
items.content:
The NHL unveiled a whole roster of alternate jerseys for this season, and the Tampa Bay Lightning's features a big skull, which you can see at center ice in the above screenshot. At first, I wondered if it was just some synergy with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, but I have since learned that it's a tribute to the city's annual Gasparilla Season, which is headlined by a pirate parade with a fraught racial past.

But does that center-ice logo look kind of uncanny to you? Maybe a little too smooth or artificial? Honestly, does it even look like ice at all? Watch the players skate over it, and see for yourself.

items.title: Texas And LSU Had A Barnburner Of Dumbass Football
items.author: Israel Daramola
items.content:
The Texas Longhorns triumphed in an exciting, last-second 22-21 victory over the LSU Tigers on Saturday, thanks to a heroic effort by QB Arch Manning and some typical breaking down of the LSU defense. But if you did not watch the contest in full, do not let the thrilling end fool you: This was some of the year's dumbest football, authored by two of our dumbest college football programs.

Let's start with the six interceptions total in this game: three for each, which is nice and neat. At first, it was LSU's Sam Leavitt throwing most of the picks, two in the first half, which makes it particularly strange that LSU was leading for the majority of this game. They were helped by the fact that Manning tossed two picks in the second half, to add to one he threw in the second quarter, and as a result the game was the Tigers' for the taking—21-10 late in the third, and still 21-16 when they punted with only 2:19 to go.

But if nothing else, Manning has shown an ability to get better when his back is against the wall. And if you're going to beat Texas, you have to stomp them out completely. Despite Manning's overall pedestrian performance, 174 yards on 19 of 35 passes, his night climaxed with the crucial touchdown. In the game's final two minutes, Manning led a 12-play, 58-yard drive down the field, culminating in a seven-yard run on third down at LSU's 11-yard line and then a four-yard TD pass to RB Raleek Brown for the go-ahead score. Cue the Texas sideline going absolutely, understandably nuts.

items.title: Did Ole Miss Simply Lack The Grit To Get To Their Game On Time?
items.author: Lauren Theisen
items.content:
On Friday, a nationwide ground stop lasting over four hours led to thousands of flight cancellations and delays from coast to coast. As a result, we're getting some Sunday afternoon college football, with No. 19 Ole Miss playing Oklahoma in Norman because they couldn't arrive on their previous schedule.

Per Ole Miss, who was flying out of Tupelo, about 50 miles from their campus in Oxford, the ground stop began just a few minutes before the team buses were scheduled to leave for the airport, at 4 p.m. Once they learned that the stop would last for hours, the players were allowed to go, and they were called for a team meeting at 8 p.m., just a little before stop was lifted. Still, it was apparently too late for them to salvage their journey that night, and the SEC ultimately pushed the game back a day as a result.

"At that hour, due to the time required to rescreen the party and travel to the Tupelo airport, the crew's duty time would have expired prior to departure," the Ole Miss statement said. "There were no other flight options at that point, and we determined it was too late to put our student-athletes on a bus trip of eight or more hours. In addition, the flight crew's duty time restrictions prevented us from being able to fly out until Saturday afternoon at the earliest."

items.title: Mauricio Pochettino Leaves The USMNT For An Even Bigger Mess
items.author: Luis Paez-Pumar
items.content:
After an extended denouement to a doomed tenure, Manchester United finally set manager Michael Carrick loose on Thursday, hoping to put an end to the club's worst league start in 40 years. On Friday, the next era for England's most famous club began, sort of, as United announced that Mauricio Pochettino would be leaving the U.S. men's national team on Nov. 18 in order to become the new boss at Old Trafford.

Carrick's departure is no surprise, but Pochettino's arrival counts as a bit of a shock. Pochettino had famously come to international prominence first at Southampton and then in his five-season-plus stint at Tottenham Hotspur, which saw that club's evolution from an also-ran into, well, an also-ran that could actually fight with the big boys. Eventually, his tenure there grew stale and the lack of trophies forced a move, with Tottenham firing him in November of 2019. The Argentine then took a year off before signing on to succeed Thomas Tuchel at Paris Saint-Germain in early 2021; his first half-season there wasn't great, as he oversaw the only PSG squad to not win the Ligue 1 title this decade. He did go on to win the league in his first full season, but PSG let him go in the summer of 2022 anyway. A return to the Premier League with Chelsea followed in 2023, where he finished in sixth place in his only season at Stamford Bridge.

That brings us to September 2024, when Pochettino became manager of the USMNT ahead of the 2026 World Cup cycle. His appointment was a big deal, as he became the highest-paid and most accomplished manager in the country's history (Jurgen Klinsmann will quibble with the latter assessment, but whatever) in advance of a home(-ish) World Cup. Pochettino had a rocky start there, but eventually righted the ship enough to guide the USMNT to a Group D first-place finish and a Round of 32 win over Bosnia and Herzegovina. An embarrassing loss to Belgium in the Round of 16 put a bit of a damper on the run, but overall, Pochettino did what he was hired to do: help the USMNT perform at the World Cup.

items.title: Utah’s Superhero Keeper Will Face Washington’s Attacking Horde
items.author: Abigail Segel

Before the NWSL playoffs started, I predicted, like many, that San Diego would go all the way. The second-seeded Wave were so solid, so well-balanced, and with a possession-based style that steamrolled team after team. Making it past the faltering, Mina Tanaka–less Utah Royals in the quarterfinals didn't feel anything close to a question. Where San Diego had earned 25 points in the final 10 matches of the regular season, Utah earned just 11.

I've never been so happy to be wrong. In delivering a 1-0 upset in San Diego last Friday, Utah provided a postseason performance that left me, a neutral, pumping with joyful adrenaline. 

As expected, San Diego dominated in nearly every way: shots, possession, touches in the final third. But the only stat that matters is goals scored, and Utah goalkeeper Mandy McGlynn had something to say about this.

items.title: Notre Dame Brings Havoc To The CFP Rankings
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
Lots of things got chucked in the bin last week: Miami's unbeaten season and Mario Cristobal's muffled rage, Ryan Day's offseason peace of mind, Lane Kiffin's shiny glow in Baton Rouge, the Heisman Trophy projections (now it's Oklahoma State quarterback Drew Mestemaker and Boise State running back Dylan Riley as the favorites, right?), Nebraska's budget for the next seven years if it fires Matt Rhule and has to pay him $63 million to turn in his sideline credential—in all, it's just getting thicker at this end of the trough.

As a result, Georgia is the new badass in residence after stomping Ole Miss, 42-7, and UCLA and Utah are last unbeaten teams in FBS. Texas is back—what, for the third time now?—and there are still five Big Ten coaches who haven't gotten the memo to rip ESPN for jerry-rigging the committee rankings to satisfy their SEC overlords. Remember, children: A conspiracy doesn't have to be proven to be advanced—it only has to sound evil to be convincing—and college football's various hierarchies have been doing Satan's bidding since 1869. But never mind all that; you're already bought in, so enjoy hell. For now, let's dance that ska.

items.title: Soccer Can Find Salvation In A Bag Of Tricks
items.author: Aaron Timms
items.content:
The suspended rabona, the showy drag with the left foot, the ricochet off the defender, the bobble of instinctive control on the byline with the right, then back onto the left for a quick push with the outstep into the goalmouth, where a teammate applies the finishing touch.

Even a few weeks later, the rabona-croqueta that Lamine Yamal improvised in Barcelona’s recent Champions League win over Galatasaray astonishes with its ingenuity. Did he intend the move to come off exactly as it did? We don’t know. Does it matter? It does not.

items.title: Would You Get Stoned With The Scythians?
items.author: Sabrina Imbler
items.content:
It's just like they told you it would happen in D.A.R.E.: You have been miraculously, tragically transported 2,800 years back in time, in the land that is now the Uyuk Valley of southern Siberia. The site will be eventually called Tunnug 1 by the archaeologists who excavate it in 2017. But that is the future, and this is the present, meaning 800 B.C. You have come to sit with the Scythians, nomads who roamed the Eurasian steppes on horseback. You have even glimpsed their warrior-king, whose long and stately braids make him seem like a pretty cool guy. Also, he's smoking. Suddenly the warrior-king glimpses you back, his reddish eyes glinting in the firelight. He leans over to you, whispers something inscrutable in an Eastern Iranic language, and extends in his grizzled hands an ancient joint, leaving you with only one question: Would you smoke that shit?

There are, to be certain, pros and cons. But one thing is clear, per a paper published recently in the journal Science: The Scythians were definitely using cannabis to get high. The analysis, led by Fabio-haired University of Bern archaeologist Gino Caspari, represents the earliest definitive evidence of humans consuming marijuana as a psychoactive drug, which was previously only traced back 2,500 years ago where Sogdian mourners once lit up in the ancient Jirzankal Cemetery in what is now western China.

It's only fitting that marijuana hails from one of the highest places in the world: the eastern Tibetan Plateau, also known as the Roof of the World. The plant evolved around 28 million years ago, and as early as 4,000 years ago Chinese farmers cultivated the plant for rope, clothing, and paper, per Science. But it is harder to tell when in the archaeological record ancient people first became gone off that loud. Wild weed, the ancestors of the domesticated kind, has only a little tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, the plant's intoxicating compound. Some researchers confirmed this when they tried to smoke wild weed and felt nothing, also per Science. (It is unclear if these particular researchers are also the paper's authors, who described cannabis as an "illicit" substance.)

items.title: Horny Nvidia CEO No Longer CEO, Possibly Still Horny
items.author: Patrick Redford
items.content:
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, who is worth over $100 billion, resigned as CEO on Thursday morning, following an emergency board meeting prompted by several reports that he'd been having various affairs, most notably with someone U.S. officials believe was spying on behalf of the Chinese government.

Nvidia has an unorthodox corporate structure, built around Huang, which largely eschews traditional executive roles in favor of a large council of vice presidents who report directly to Huang, which makes the matter of his succession trickier to game out than it would be in other cases of a CEO doing sex stuff. He'll be succeeded on an interim basis by Colette Kress, formerly the CFO, whom Wired characterizes as one of the few people with a high-level grasp of the company's finances and ties to Wall Street.

A quick recap of how we got here: Nvidia is the single most important hardware technology company in the world, a chip designer that boosted its market cap to more than $4 trillion by making the must-have picks and shovels of the ongoing AI boom. As such, Nvidia is something like a shadow arm of the U.S. government, the latter of which is engaged in the stupidest-ever version of the space race with China over who can build the machine god first. Nvidia wants to sell its best stuff to Chinese companies because it doesn't really care who wins, as long as it makes money for investors, but the Trump administration won't allow it. Meanwhile, the tip-top Chinese AI companies have found ways to smuggle in the best Nvidia chips via third parties mostly based in Southeast Asia.

items.title: How I Succumbed To Reef Madness And Came To Love A Slowly Sinking Ship
items.author: Dave McKenna
items.content:
The SS United States finally sank in the Gulf of Mexico at around 10 p.m. ET Wedneday night. Not since the Minnow had a doomed vessel’s last tour run so far over schedule and still kept viewers engaged. Those who stuck with the 10-hour livestream were rewarded with an amazingly touching denouement. 

The ship had its day. The SS United States hit the seas in 1952, and at 990 feet long was about 100 feet longer than the Titanic, yet was able to hit speeds of more than 38 knots, still faster than any transatlantic ocean liner ever. But it was deemed obsolete and taken out of service way back in 1969, and spent the last 30 years docked in Philadelphia. Attempts to keep the SS US above water as a hotel or museum failed, and some folks in Okaloosa County, Florida, decided the liner was most valuable at the bottom of sea. The county floated a $10 million plan to turn the ship into an artificial reef and thereby enhance the Redneck Riviera’s reputation as a fishing and scuba diving destination. This entailed sinking the SS US about 22 miles off Fort Walton Beach during the very same week that the Edmund Fitzgerald hit bottom 51 years earlier.

items.title: ‘Mario Vargas Llosa: A Life’ Is Dishy And Definitive
items.author: Max Pearl
items.content:
Mario Vargas Llosa: A Life might seem like a bland title for a biography, until it dawns on you exactly how much living the man did. He eloped with his aunt at 19, then humiliated her by writing a novel about it translated into more than 30 languages; divorced her for her much younger niece, his first cousin; and, after a scandalous 50-year marriage beset by separations, walked out one last time for the Spanish socialite and tabloid favorite Isabel Preysler, ex-wife of Julio Iglesias and mother of Enrique.

Arguably the world’s most famous Peruvian after Paddington, Vargas Llosa would have been president if not for the dark-horse populist Alberto Fujimori—father of the current president—who handily defeated Vargas Llosa’s platform of neoliberal shock economics in 1990. And in 2010, at age 74, he won the Nobel Prize in Literature, joining the pantheon alongside his lifelong frenemy Gabriel García Márquez, whom he famously punched in the face at a film premiere, for reasons that remain unclear. 

Thus, the page count of the new biography—the first since his death in 2025 and almost certainly the last word on the subject—clocking in at 812. Gerald Martin, a British critic who also wrote the definitive book on García Márquez, spent 25 years interviewing Vargas Llosa and those who knew him. The result is a monumental achievement: a synthesis of his subject's personal and political life with a surgical yet shockingly breezy analysis of the writing itself. And while it’s not always right to conflate fictional characters with their creator, Vargas Llosa is a special case, Martin argues: a novelist who peppered his work with confessions.

items.title: New House Minority Leader Still Faces Old Questions On Ohio State Sexual Abuse
items.author: Diana Moskovitz
items.content:
House Republicans elected Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio this week as their new minority leader. He won 106-73 on a secret ballot. Those who follow politics will know his name as a staunch Donald Trump ally who served as chairman of the Freedom Caucus, voted to overturn the 2020 presidential election results, and ignored a subpoena from the House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 insurrection.

Jordan previously ran for the role of Speaker of the House in 2023 but failed three times to get a majority of the votes needed. This too was voted on by secret ballot. At the time, those who did speak about their "no" votes told NPR they voted against Jordan because of bullying and threats being made to them and their families by either Jordan or Jordan supporters.

But at that time, Jordan also was continuing to face questions about his connection to Ohio State's sexual abuse scandal. In 2018, former wrestlers for the university came forward, saying they had been sexually abused by a team doctor under the guise of him providing them with medical treatment, usually during a physical exam. The wrestlers forced an independent investigation, and the ensuing published report said that Dr. Richard Strauss sexually abused "at least 177 male student-patients" at Ohio State, many of them while he worked in the athletics department from the late 1970s until 1998. Strauss died by suicide in 2005.

items.title: The Oilers Are A Bunch Of Squirts And A Couple Of Gods
items.author: Lauren Theisen
items.content:
For the second goal of the Oilers' 3-2 win over the Philadelphia Flyers, the NHL's best offense converted yet another power play. Zero points for guessing the man who picked up the primary assist: Connor McDavid now has a 15-dish lead over the next-highest guy on the league's assist leaderboard, as well as a 12-point lead in overall points. The next two guys on the latter list, by the way, are both Oilers, too.

With the score 1-0 in the second period, and Oliver Bonk serving a two-minute penalty for bonking (OK, fine, interference), McDavid captured the defense's attention by skating with the puck far out on the left in the attacking zone. In doing so, he was able to give his teammate Zach Hyman a little bit of personal space right in front of the crease. This is the part that he made look easy: He fired a quick centering pass through two alert Flyers and got the puck to an awkward spot right at goalie Dan Vladar's knees. Hyman just had to poke his stick around in there to encourage the biscuit over the line.

items.title: Why Do People Keep Cheating At Marathons?
items.author: Patrick Redford
items.content:
When asked why he kept trying to climb Mt. Everest, the climber George Mallory famously replied, "Because it's there." When asked about his creative process, SimCity creator Will Wright said, "I don't know. I thought it would be cool." I've always been struck by the inscrutability of inspiration, by the notion that we can't always explain why we do the things we do. This week's episode of Only If You Get Caught gets into this psychic terrain by way of examining the question of why so many people cheat at marathons.

The premise of the show is that cheating can most often be understood as a rational calculation. Someone chooses to break the rules because they ultimately decide that the benefit of getting away with it outweighs the downside of getting caught. But cutting the course on a marathon doesn't fit into this heuristic. Most marathon cheaters don't really cheat for anything, at least not anything that matches up to the shame and derision that comes with being exposed as a cheater. This dynamic is especially true these days, when cheaters both are easier to catch and have less to gain. In late September, an influencer was caught hitching a ride on a bike at the Berlin Marathon en route to posting the unremarkable time of 4:53:46.

Taken as a whole, marathon cheating suggests that there's an unscratchable itch, a desire to break the rules for the simple sake of doing it. To break it all down, I drafted in our old friend Dennis Young, whom you may know from his time with us at the old site or for his current work editing Front Office Sports. Dennis is great, and we had a fun time getting into it.

items.title: Call Her Petty
items.author: Kelsey McKinney
items.content:
In the fall of 2018, Alexandra Cooper and Sofia Franklyn released the first episode of Call Her Daddy by introducing themselves. “To be honest, I’m probably here just to ride Alex’s coattails,” Franklyn said. Cooper, more confident on mic in sound and delivery, declares herself a “stay-at-home, try-hard vlogger by day and an Insta-hoe by night.” The show, which at the time focused on their sex lives, drug habits, and bad decisions, exploded in popularity. They signed a three-year deal with Barstool Sports that year.

Call Her Daddy was so popular that the duo tried to renegotiate that contract in 2020, and their friendship quickly deteriorated and became a mess of tabloid headlines and legal threats. Franklyn claimed that Cooper went behind her back and betrayed her. Cooper claimed that Franklyn was uncooperative in negotiations and deployed her boyfriend Peter Nelson (who was an HBO Sports executive at the time) to make things more difficult.

The podcast’s IP remained controlled by Barstool, and Cooper took the reins fully in May of 2020. If you look at the Call Her Daddy YouTube page, that is the beginning of history. The episodes with Franklyn, the first two years of content, are gone. Cooper has moved on. In 2021, she left Barstool and signed a $60 million contract with Spotify. In 2024, she signed a $125 million contract with Sirius XM. Call Her Daddy has evolved from a sex chat romp to one of the biggest podcasts in the world. Cooper has interviewed Kamala Harris, Michelle Obama, Kim Kardashian, and dozens of other major celebrities. The podcast, along with her persona, is softer, less raunchy, and more grown-up.

items.title: Dianna Russini’s Return To Sports Media Was A Bit Of A Disaster
items.author: Tom Ley
items.content:
This week marked Dianna Russini's return to public life. The former highly compensated NFL reporter, who blew up her career by canoodling in public with Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel, began her return from disgrace the way a lot of notable people who can afford capable PR firms do: with a soft-focus profile in People. The next phase of her comeback, Wednesday's premiere of her new weekly football show on BetUS TV, was not so competently executed.

The People article is about what you'd expect. Russini talks about how "heartbreaking" the the last six months have been, and how having to resign from The Athletic after going interlaced-fingers mode with Vrabel at an adults-only resort was a "nightmare." Russini also seems to be maintaining her position that there was nothing inappropriate about her relationship with Vrabel, which included rendezvous in a bar, a casino, and on a boat. She complained to People about all the "lies" that "became so out of control.” The profile finished up with Russini trying to reposition herself as an inspiration to women. “I really hope that I can be someone other women see: you can pick yourself up, get back in there and not be afraid,” she said.

With that out of the way, it was time for the main event. The Russini Report, a weekly one-hour web show about the NFL, debuted on Wednesday. The show is hosted by BetUS, which is a sketchy offshore sportsbook that is headquartered in Costa Rica and regulated by the government of Curaçao. items.title: An Expert And A Noob Play ‘Final Fantasy Resonance’
items.author: Barry Petchesky
items.content:
While there are many fantastic Japanese role-playing game (JRPG, for short) series out there, and with apologies to Dragon Quest and Persona, Final Fantasy is the biggest and most important of them all. Every numbered entry in the main series is an event, and since almost every game is its own story (to date, there have been two main games to get direct sequels: X got X-2, and XIII inexplicably got two sequels), there are swaths of new gamers dipping in every time a new game releases.

Despite that, it's safe to say that Final Fantasy has somewhat lost its way, or at least what was once its identity. What started as a turn-based RPG has evolved, first into a more active-style combat system and then more recently into something bordering on an action game. This makes sense for Square Enix, the series's developer, as turn-based combat has mostly, though not entirely, slipped from an important game genre into something more niche. Chasing the action trend that took over turn-based RPG's spot with the Soulsborne games made financial sense, and it kept Final Fantasy from growing stale.

That said, there's still a hunger for turn-based RPGs, and especially turn-based Final Fantasy games; the last mainline game to be strictly turn-based was 2001's X. With that in mind, we arrive at Final Fantasy Resonance, the recently released (and relatively successful) spin-off that is a sort of remake/re-using of assets of Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, a mobile gacha game. Resonance is not asking the player to part with any money besides the initial price tag, and instead is a fully fleshed-out 30-to-40-hour turn-based RPG adventure through time, space, and Final Fantasy history.

items.title: Paul George Has Turned Out To Be The Ur-Celtic
items.author: Giri Nathan
items.content:
Get past the unseasoned beef between Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown in Tuesday's Celtics-Sixers matchup, and reach instead for the real juice: a killer performance by Paul George, the player for whom Brown was traded. Though a single regular-season game in November is no way useful to assess a trade in its entirety, the contrast last night between those two wings was telling: Brown (keyed-up, foul-prone, poor decision-making) sat out much of a game where George (methodical, efficient, at ease in the flow of offense) flourished. Boston won, 123-101. More than anything, George's 36-point outing was a reminder of his eerily slick, timeless style could have plugged into every NBA roster constructed over the last decade, and how it distills Joe Mazzulla's Celtics squad to its spiritual essence.

Fair minds were skeptical that a star version of George would ever return. In two years with Philly, he seemed to have receded into a fog of lower-body injuries, mystery drug use, and inconsistent podcasting, playing just 78 total regular-season games. Meanwhile, Brown had just come off a workhorse campaign for the Celtics, logging 71 games while soaking up 36 percent usage on his way to an All-NBA second team. For all the hand-wringing about Brown's true value, both in a vacuum and within the Celtics system, he was clearly the more valuable player at the time of the trade. When swapping two seemingly onerous contracts for one another, each one asking somewhere between 32 and 35 percent of the salary cap for a wing who likely wouldn't live up to that price tag, it was the Sixers who had to sweeten the deal with draft picks.

items.title: Two Hard-Up Vikings Fans “Celebrate” The Return Of Kirk Cousins
items.author: Drew Magary
items.content:
Three years ago, after a long but loveless marriage, the Minnesota Vikings let QB Kirk Cousins walk out the door. They felt free. Unburdened. Hopeful, even. No longer would they have to spend night after night asking themselves, “Where is this relationship going?” They could finally find someone new. They could believe in love again, and maybe even have a bit of fun getting back out there on the scene.

That scene, much to the Vikings’ chagrin, turned out to be far less exciting than they’d anticipated. Maybe it was them. Maybe they weren’t quite as charming and attractive as they thought they’d been. Regardless, they eventually found themselves lonely, broken, and frankly hard up. And so, with Taylor Swift’s “Style” playing on a loop in the background, they swallowed their pride, along with a good amount of red wine, and made the call they swore they’d never make. Kirk Cousins is a Viking again, and us Vikings fans feel a little bit ashamed that we let this happen all over again. That’s the subject of this week’s special Trade Deadline Edition of All Ball.

items.title: Look Who Came Crawling Back To Kirk Cousins
items.author: Ray Ratto
items.content:
Under any other circumstances, in any other year, Kirk Cousins being traded back to the Minnesota Vikings would be universally mocked under the You Can't Make Someone Go Back Home statutes. The story of Kirk and the Vikes is one that had been told all the way through, in no great rush at that, and was on the merits not one that would have had the public demanding or even imagining a reboot. But here, now, in the situation in which the Vikings have placed themselves—well, put it this way: No NFL trade has ever had so many people call their shot ahead of time and then nod with approval after it came to pass.

Yes, even though Cousins already titillated and frustrated the Vikings alternately over six years by being Almost That Guy, they brought him back on Tuesday in a desperate admission that they had turned their quarterback room into a lividly radioactive dump site. Cousins, we must presume, went with a song in his heart, because he finally found his nirvana: a place without a young quarterback desperate to make his bones waiting to replace him.

A Cousins trade of some kind had been rumored from the moment he landed in Las Vegas to play for the Raiders, primarily because he was so obviously there to hold the place card until No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza was ready to replace him. Minnesota wasn't much of a trade option until the Vikings made themselves one—well, the only one. After Cousins was lured to Atlanta (illegally, as the league eventually ruled), the Vikings fell in and out of love with J.J. McCarthy, fell briefly in like with Kyler Murray and then watched his hamstring explode, watched Carson Wentz melt into a puddle in real time on Monday night, and rejected Max Brosmer as a viable option on the fly.
